card.name: Loyalty dance
card.tagline: A collective mass dance performed to display political devotion during the Cultural Revolution.
card.profile: The loyalty dance (Zhongzi wu) was a collective mass dance performed in public spaces across China during the Cultural Revolution in the late 1960s. Designed as a key fixture of Chairman Mao Zedong's cult of personality, it incorporated simple body movements adapted from folk dance traditions of Xinjiang. Danced by citizens of all ages and backgrounds, the movements centered on expressive gestures of devotion directed toward portraits of Mao and the sky. Accompanied by revolutionary songs like 'The East is Red,' the tradition reached its height around 1968 before rapidly fading after the Cultural Revolution ended.
card.insight: During the late 1960s, everyone from office workers to elderly women with bound feet was expected to perform the loyalty dance in public squares, stretching their arms from their hearts toward portraits of Chairman Mao.
card.profile_long:
The loyalty dance, known in Chinese as Zhōngzì wǔ, emerged in the late 1960s following the outbreak of the Cultural Revolution in 1966. Developed as an integral component of Chairman Mao Zedong's cult of personality, the dance functioned as a public, standardized expression of political discipline and total personal devotion. By 1968, the movement reached a climax under the banner of the 'Three Loyalties'—mandating loyalty to Chairman Mao, Mao Zedong Thought, and Chairman Mao's revolutionary line. Public squares, plazas, and street parades became setting stages where compliance and reverence were demonstrated en masse.

The dance relied on accessible, repetitive choreography derived originally from a folk dance popular in Xinjiang. Its defining physical gesture involved stretching one's arms outward from the heart toward a portrait of Mao, alternating with movements directed upward to the sky to symbolize elevated respect for the leader. Because the dance was intended as a universal obligation rather than a specialized artistic display, participation was required across all social classes. Miners, office workers, young toddlers, and even elderly women with bound feet engaged in the daily performance of the routine in public spaces.

Musical accompaniment consisted of ubiquitous revolutionary songs of the era. Tracks such as 'The East is Red' (Dōngfāng hóng), 'Beloved Chairman Mao,' 'Golden Hill of Beijing,' and 'Sailing the Seas Depends on the Helmsman' provided the rhythmic backing for the mass performances. Lyrics explicitly reinforced political themes, including quotations from Mao and declarations that devotion to the leader superseded traditional familial ties. These songs created a uniform, structured soundtrack across cities and rural communities alike.

Following the 9th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in April 1969, the widespread requirement and popularity of the loyalty dance began to wane. By the early 1970s, public performances became rare, and with the formal end of the Cultural Revolution in 1976, the loyalty dance disappeared entirely from daily public life in China.

sections.origins_and_history: The loyalty dance appeared soon after the Cultural Revolution started in 1966. In the late 1960s, Chairman Mao's cult of personality reached new heights, leading to citizens performing the dance to express political loyalty. By 1968, 'Three Loyalties' activities reached a climax in various areas, making the dance widespread all over the country. After the 9th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in April 1969, the dance gradually declined in popularity, became rare by the 1970s, and rapidly disappeared as the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance consisted of a simple collective dance performed in public places like plazas, squares, or at parades. Choreographically, it did not involve much more than stretching one's arms from the heart to Mao's portrait, with basic movements originating from a folk dance popular in Xinjiang. Hand and arm movements were consistently directed toward the sky, symbolizing respect for Mao Zedong. Participation was universal and expected of miners, office workers, toddlers, and elderly women with bound feet.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was frequently accompanied by revolutionary songs. Key songs included 'The East is Red' (东方红), 'Beloved Chairman Mao' (敬愛的毛主席), 'Golden Hill of Beijing' (北京的金山上), and 'Sailing the Seas Depends on the Helmsman' (大海航行靠舵手), alongside musical settings featuring quotations from Chairman Mao. Lyrics reinforced the political nature of the performance, emphasizing collective worship and loyalty.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances took place in everyday public settings including open plazas, public squares, and street parades. Performers wore standard daily clothing, as participation encompassed ordinary citizens from all walks of life, including industrial miners, office workers, young children, and elderly women.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was an everyday fixture of life in the late 1960s, practiced to display lifelong devotion to Mao Zedong and exercise total discipline. It was closely linked to the ideological slogan of the 'Three Loyalties' (三忠于): loyalty to Chairman Mao, loyalty to Mao Zedong Thought, and loyalty to Chairman Mao's revolutionary line. Song lyrics performed during the dance asserted that relationship with Mao was closer than that with one's own parents.
sections.notable_figures: The central figure inspiring the dance was Chairman Mao Zedong, whose portrait served as the visual focal point for the physical gestures of the dancers.
sections.lineage: The movement technique originated from a folk dance popular in Xinjiang, adapted during the Cultural Revolution into a simplified collective mass dance.

claims.text: The loyalty dance was a collective public dance during the Cultural Revolution in China.
The dance involved stretching arms from the heart to Mao's portrait and incorporated Xinjiang folk dance movements.
Performances were accompanied by specific revolutionary songs like 'The East is Red'.
People of all ages and backgrounds including miners, toddlers, and elderly women with bound feet were expected to dance.
Arm movements were directed toward the sky to show respect for Mao.
